title: Under-keel clearance: how much water is really under your ship?

scenes.label: MARITIME INSIGHT
scenes.heading: How much water is really under your keel?
scenes.narration: Charted depth minus draught is not your real clearance. Here is what is missing.

scenes.heading: UKC
scenes.body: Under-keel clearance: the vertical distance between the lowest point of the hull and the seabed
scenes.narration: UKC means under keel clearance: the vertical distance between the lowest point of your hull and the seabed.

scenes.label: THE CALCULATION
scenes.heading: Depth of water, less draught, less squat
scenes.narration: Take the charted depth and add the height of tide. Subtract your deepest static draught. Then subtract squat, because a ship sinks deeper as her speed increases, especially in shallow water.

scenes.label: WHAT ELSE REDUCES IT
scenes.heading: The margin is smaller than you think

items.title: Heel in a turn
items.text: A wide ship gains draught quickly when she heels

items.title: Swell and waves
items.text: Heave and pitch use up clearance

items.title: Chart accuracy
items.text: Check the CATZOC of the area

scenes.narration: Other things reduce it further: heel when turning, swell, the accuracy of the chart, and a change in water density. Your company policy sets the minimum you must keep.

scenes.label: KEY TAKEAWAY
scenes.heading: Small margin? Slow down. Less speed, less squat.
scenes.narration: Calculate it for every critical part of the passage, and if the margin is small, slow down.

sources.title: Resolution A.893(21): Guidelines for voyage planning

meta.description: Under-keel clearance is more than charted depth minus draught. Tide, squat, heel, swell, chart accuracy and water density all change the real margin. A practical explanation for deck officers.
